'''Eastern Abenaki''' is an extinct [[Algonquian languages|Algonquian language]] formerly spoken by the [[Abenaki]] people. They were spoken by several peoples, including the [[Penobscot]] of what is now [[Maine]]. Other speakers of Eastern Abenaki included tribes such as the [[Androscoggin people|Amoscocongon]] who spoke the Arosagunticook dialect,<ref>{{cite web |title=Arosaguntacook Indian Tribe |url=http://www.native-languages.org/definitions/androscoggin.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240109205330/http://www.native-languages.org/definitions/androscoggin.htm |archive-date=Jan 9, 2024 |access-date=Jan 9, 2024 |website=Native Languages}}</ref> and the [[Norridgewock|Caniba]], which are documented in French-language materials from the colonial period. The last known natively fluent speaker of Penobscot Abenaki, Madeline Shay, died in 1993.<ref>{{cite web |title=Penobscot |url=http://www.native-languages.org/penobscot.htm |access-date=October 25, 2011 |work=Native Languages of the Americas}}</ref><ref name = e16/> However, several Penobscot elders still speak Penobscot, and there is an ongoing effort to preserve it and teach it in the local schools;<ref>{{cite web |title=Penobscot |url=http://www.abbemuseum.org/headline-news/Language/HeadlineNewsLanguage%20Penobscot.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160320153919/http://www.abbemuseum.org/headline-news/Language/HeadlineNewsLanguage%20Penobscot.html |archive-date=March 20, 2016 |access-date=Feb 21, 2016 |website=Abbe Museum}}</ref> much of the language was preserved by [[Frank Siebert]].<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Gregory |first=Alice |date=April 19, 2021 |title=How did a self-taught linguist come to own an indigenous language? |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2021/04/19/how-did-a-self-taught-linguist-come-to-own-an-indigenous-language |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412110531/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2021/04/19/how-did-a-self-taught-linguist-come-to-own-an-indigenous-language |archive-date=2021-04-12 |magazine=The New Yorker}}</ref> About 500 Penobscot words are still being used in the community in everyday language such as ''Muhmum'' for 'grandpa' and ''nolke'' for 'deer'.<ref name="bangordailynewsjuly20132">{{cite news |last=McCrea |first=Nick |date=July 11, 2013 |title=Penobscot Nation, UMaine win grants to help revive tribe's language |url=http://bangordailynews.com/2013/07/11/news/penobscot/penobscot-nation-umaine-win-grants-to-help-revive-tribes-language/ |access-date=23 July 2013 |newspaper=Bangor Daily News}}</ref> 

In July 2013, the Penobscot Nation, the [[University of Maine]] and the [[American Philosophical Society]] received a grant from the [[National Endowment for the Humanities]] to expand and publish the first Penobscot Dictionary.<ref name="bangordailynewsjuly20132" />
